Two Natures of Christ
too NAY-cherz of KRYST
n. phrase (Christological doctrine)
From the Chalcedonian Definition (AD 451), which settled the language of Christology: one Person (hypostasis), two natures (physeis)—divine and human—existing without confusion, change, division, or separation. The four Greek adverbs of Chalcedon have defined the limits of orthodox Christology ever since.

See also: Two Natures of Christ

Biblical Definition

The doctrine of Christ's two natures teaches that Jesus Christ is one Person who possesses, completely and without diminishment, both a divine nature and a human nature. John declares that the eternal Word “became flesh”—not that He traded deity for humanity, but that He added humanity to Himself (John 1:14). Paul teaches that He “existed in the form of God” and yet “emptied Himself, taking the form of a bondservant, being made in the likeness of men” (Phil 2:6–7). The emptying (kenôsis) was not a subtraction of deity but a veiling of divine glory in genuine human flesh. Because the children share in flesh and blood, He Himself likewise partook of the same—not by becoming less God, but by becoming truly man (Heb 2:14). The apostolic test of orthodoxy was precisely this: “every spirit that confesses Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is from God” (1 John 4:2). The Council of Chalcedon (451 AD) gave the church its permanent vocabulary: the two natures are united in one Person without confusion (the divine and human remain distinct), without change (neither nature is altered), without division (they are not separate persons), and without separation (they are not loosely joined). This “four-adverb formula” has defined orthodoxy for fifteen centuries. The 1689 London Baptist Confession (8.2) affirms it without reservation.

Webster 1828 Definition

The Chalcedonian teaching that Jesus Christ possesses a complete divine nature and a complete human nature in one undivided Person—without confusion, change, division, or separation—the cornerstone of fifteen centuries of orthodox Christology.

TWO NATURES OF CHRIST, n. phrase. The confessional Christological doctrine, settled at the Council of Chalcedon (AD 451), that Jesus Christ is one Person in two natures—divine and human.

The divine nature is the same nature the Son has shared with the Father and Spirit from eternity: omniscient, omnipotent, omnipresent, immutable, impassible. The human nature is a true, complete human nature—body and soul—taken from the Virgin Mary, capable of growth, suffering, and death.

The four Chalcedonian adverbs define the limits: the natures are united without confusion (never fused into a third thing), without change (neither nature is transformed), without division (one Person, not two persons), without separation (not merely morally united but ontologically one).

Errors that the definition guards against: Nestorianism (two persons loosely conjoined, corrected by ‘without division’), Eutychianism (the two natures fused into one mixed nature, corrected by ‘without confusion’), Monophysitism (only one nature after the union, corrected by ‘without change’).

The practical import: only a truly divine Savior can bear infinite wrath; only a truly human Savior can serve as substitute for human sinners. Both natures are necessary for the atonement to hold.

Key Scripture

John 1:14 — "And the Word became flesh. He pitched His tent among us, and we saw His glory with our own eyes — the glory of the Father's one-and-only Son, full of grace and full of truth."

Philippians 2:6–7 — "who, although He existed in the form of God, did not regard equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied Himself, taking the form of a bondservant, being made in the likeness of men."

Hebrews 2:14 — "Therefore, since the children share in flesh and blood — He Himself likewise also partook of the same — so that through death He might render powerless him who had the power of death, that is, the devil."

1 John 4:2 — "By this you know the Spirit of God: every spirit that confesses Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is from God."

Modern Corruption

Every Christological heresy attacks one of the two natures or their union: Arianism denies the full deity; Docetism denies the full humanity; Nestorianism divides the Person; Eutychianism confuses the natures. Modern functional Christologies repeat these ancient errors in new vocabulary.

expand to see more

Ancient heresies remain the template for modern errors. Arianism (Son is a lesser God) and Docetism (the Son only appeared human) strike at one nature each. Eutychianism (the natures merged into a hybrid) and Nestorianism (two persons conjoined) strike at the union. Modern Christologies that treat Jesus as a uniquely Spirit-filled man (adoptionism dressed in progressive evangelical vocabulary) are functional Docetism—they confess human flesh but deny the eternal divine Person who assumed it. Process theology, which pictures a God who grows and suffers along with creation, effectively produces a single mixed nature incapable of atoning for sin.

The pastoral danger is not always academic. When the two natures are separated in preaching—so that “the divine Jesus” works miracles while “the human Jesus” suffers alone—the unity of the Person is practically denied. The Chalcedonian formula guards against this: what is done is done by the one Person, in and through both natures. The cross is not the suffering of a mere man; it is the suffering of God the Son in the humanity He assumed. That is why the blood of Calvary has infinite worth.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek physis (nature, essence) applied by the Council of Chalcedon (451 AD) to the Incarnation: the Son took on a second, full human nature without surrendering His divine nature.

expand to see more

Greek physis — nature, essence, the intrinsic character of a being; Chalcedon defined Christ as en duo physesin (in two natures).

Greek hypostasis — Person, subsistence; Chalcedon taught one hypostasis (Person) possessing the two natures without confusion.

Greek a-syn-khuths — without confusion; the first Chalcedonian adverb, excluding fusion of the two natures.

Greek a-diairetôs — without division; the third adverb, excluding any split of the one Person into two.

Latin communicatio idiomatum — the communication of attributes; the doctrine that predicates proper to either nature can be spoken of the one Person.

Usage

"A Savior with only one nature cannot save: a purely divine being cannot die as human substitute; a purely human being cannot bear infinite divine wrath."

"The two natures are united in the one Person, so what the Son does in His humanity He does as God the Son—giving infinite value to His obedience, suffering, and resurrection."

"The Chalcedonian formula is not speculative philosophy but faithful exegesis: John 1:14, Phil 2:6–7, and Heb 2:14 require exactly the categories Chalcedon provides."
